- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.

Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups

# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)

- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally reports a league-wide study, "under review" at the time of the talk, using public MLB data (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Window:** 2004 to 2014, chosen so that players who had surgery in 2014 had time to return (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Counts:** about 200 surgeries, and on average 180 days of MLB-calendar time missed (z_6M5r7031A [12:14]). About half the players were starters and half relievers, with a small proportion of closers (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Total:** adjusted to 2017 levels, "half a billion dollars" of salary lost over the period to rehab alone (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Excluded:** medical, travel and rehab costs; downtime before the surgery; lost team wins; trade value; and every minor league player (z_6M5r7031A [12:44] to [13:44]). He speculates the full cost might be 1 billion or 1.5 billion and says "I don't know" (z_6M5r7031A [13:44]).
- **Per player:** medical cost of about $50,000, which he calls conservative (z_6M5r7031A [11:13]). (Untested: bare assertion, no method given.)
- **Salary per WAR:** it "balloons" after surgery and does not return to the pre-surgery level until 3 years after the pitcher returns (z_6M5r7031A [10:43]). In Q&A he calls the salary-over-WAR calculation "relatively back of the envelope" and not adjusted (z_6M5r7031A [28:27]). (Untested: back-of-envelope, unadjusted.)

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism; this is an accounting of public salary data. Inference: it counts only direct salary during rehab, which is why the number is a floor on the speaker's own account.

**When to apply** — As an example of costing an injury type from public records by counting time missed and attaching a value. Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a Baylor version would count games and practices missed by injury type and position group with Athletic Medicine, with no salary figure.

**When NOT to apply** — The study was under review, not published, at the time. Baylor athletes have no player salaries, so dollar figures and dollars per WAR do not transfer to college. The salary-per-WAR calculation is unadjusted and the speaker's own words are "back of the envelope." The 180-day figure is MLB calendar time. It is professional baseball pitchers only, and it counts surgeries, not all injuries.

**Example** — The speaker's own: about 200 surgeries over 2004 to 2014 and 180 MLB-calendar days missed on average, summing to half a billion 2017 dollars (z_6M5r7031A [12:14] to [12:44]).

143:- No formal injury-risk model (ACWR, tissue-capacity tracking, a biomechanical screening protocol with defined red flags) is attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; the detailed treatment of ACWR and injury-risk modeling that does exist (Clemson curriculum) is reference material only, not confirmed Baylor practice. Rehab and RTP: role stated (Q4, Q22) and a written protocol exists in the UE and LE templates (Q4a), not yet staged. Coaching stays thin: constraints-led coaching is not used (Q25), and the rest is unclaimed course material.

Yet ACWR is still looked at ("We dabble with ACWR") though he does not "trust it for anything", and movement screens are "just collected" without changing decisions (Q12). Inference: by his own rule both are candidates to retire or to be given a question.

# Circadian Timing Changed Game Results: West Coast Evening NFL Teams and East Coast Baseball Teams

**What it is** — The speaker (unnamed in the captions) lays out a general premise: physiological functions that affect performance, such as best coordination, fastest reaction time, greatest cardiovascular efficiency and muscle strength, tend to peak in the evening (J7smyg1Czik [13:49]). Evidence cited for games. NFL: "my colleagues Smith and motra" (caption spelling) examined 40 years of NFL data on evening games between East Coast and West Coast teams, and found the West Coast beat the Las Vegas point spread and won "twice as often," with no significant difference in daytime games (J7smyg1Czik [14:19], [14:49]). The speaker calls it robust and says it accounts for team quality and travel, so the homeostatic (time awake) drive does not explain it (J7smyg1Czik [14:49], [15:20]). Baseball: a study about five or six years before the talk (J7smyg1Czik [15:20]) found that crossing three time zones raised the chance of losing the first game, "60% or more" in the captions (unclear); and that East Coast teams returning home lost their home advantage, about 3.9%, when playing away teams from the same time zone (J7smyg1Czik [15:50], [16:20]). The speaker also says morning-type pitchers pitch better in day games and night-type pitchers in evening games (J7smyg1Czik [15:50]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that every physiological function has a circadian rhythm and each body's clock peaks at a time of day; a team playing at its own biological peak has an advantage (J7smyg1Czik [13:49], [14:49]). The speaker treats the NFL result as the circadian effect alone because the analysis controls for travel and team quality. The description of the controls is brief.

**When to apply** — As a scheduling consideration for evening games and travel across time zones. Inference: for a team that travels across time zones for a game, this supports timing meals, sleep and training to the local clock where the schedule allows. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q23): "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." (Explicit, interview-confirmed; method-baseline.md says nothing on travel). In-season game week: lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game (Q15, Explicit).

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: both studies are second-hand and uncited (authors caption-spelled, no journal or year for the NFL study). The NFL study is described by the speaker; its method is not shown beyond "controls for team quality and travel," and the authors are caption-spelled. The baseball numbers are garbled in the captions ("60% or more" and 3.9% are unclear whether they are probabilities, percent changes or percentage points). NFL evening games are professional, with specific travel patterns; college football kickoff times, travel and east-west mixes differ and were not studied. The result is about averages across teams and does not tell you which individual players are affected. Existing library guidance on athlete sleep and jet lag is an expert consensus, not a game-outcomes study.

**Example** — The speaker's own: West Coast teams winning evening games against East Coast teams about twice as often, with no difference in daytime games, over 40 years (J7smyg1Czik [14:19], [14:49]).

**Related** — [[framework--classify-chronotype-and-time-peak-performance]]; [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/vitale-2026-from-gpt-4-to-expert-endorsed-athlete-guidance-a-delphi-consensus-on-sleep-and-jet-lag]].
=== claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it.md
---

# Sleep Deficits Accumulate, and Three Nights of Recovery Sleep Do Not Fully Erase Them

**What it is** — The speaker, a sleep scientist (unnamed in the captions) who elsewhere in the talk says "our lab at Henry Ford" (J7smyg1Czik [07:42]), says that getting six to seven hours instead of eight "doubles or triples" normal reaction time, which the talk puts at about a quarter of a second (J7smyg1Czik [01:33]). The talk shows a sleep deprivation study in which the same individuals go through different conditions: seven days of 7 hours in bed per the captions (the summary phrase "7 five versus 3 hours" is garbled) versus nine hours in bed, each followed by three days of nine-hour recovery sleep (J7smyg1Czik [02:05], [02:36]). Mean speed and the number of lapses worsened as days of deficit increased; after three recovery days at nine hours in bed, the restricted group recovered but "never as good as" people who get nine hours regularly (J7smyg1Czik [02:36]). The speaker concludes that deficits are cumulative and "non-recoverable" over a short window, so sleep before a game is not enough (J7smyg1Czik [22:33]), and says athletes tend to sleep poorly right before games because of anxiety or a strange environment (J7smyg1Czik [03:07]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for accumulation; the study result is shown without one. Inference: the result as stated means a short recovery block does not return performance to the level of consistently well-rested people, so the amount of regular sleep leading up to an event matters more than the last night.

**When to apply** — When advising athletes before a competition or travel block: focus on sleep across the preceding days, not only the night before. Inference: this supports looking at multi-night sleep, if it were measured. Eric's baseline: recovery is managed through training-load design alone and nothing objective is tracked, sleep included (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit). The talk's finding would need some sleep measure to act on; none exists in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — The study is not cited, and its sample size, population and test are not stated; the design numbers are garbled in the captions (7 hours in bed as captioned, "7 five versus 3 hours"). Confidence is untested. "Non-recoverable" is the speaker's wording for a three-day test; the talk does not follow recovery beyond three days. Auto-caption talk from 2017; the results were presented by a speaker with a sleep-lab affiliation, not as a peer-reviewed table. It does not apply as a measurement tool: it shows an effect in healthy adults under restriction, not a sleep target for Baylor athletes.

**Example** — The speaker's own: restricted-time-in-bed participants after three nine-hour recovery nights compared with participants who had nine hours throughout (J7smyg1Czik [02:36]).

**Related** — [[claim--sleep-extension-improved-stanford-athlete-performance]]; [[heuristic--weekend-sleep-extension-signals-a-deficit]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]] (NCAA Division I sleep and nap behavior).
=== claim--sleep-extension-improved-stanford-athlete-performance.md
---

# Extending Time in Bed to Ten Hours for Six Weeks Improved Stanford Athletes' Performance

**What it is** — The speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) summarizes the Stanford sleep-extension studies: athletes were given 10 hours in bed for six weeks, wore actigraphs, kept sleep diaries, and were tested near the end of the six weeks (J7smyg1Czik [09:12], [09:42]). Reported results: basketball players had a significant reduction in sprint times and a 9% increase in both free throws and three-point field goals, were less sleepy, and rated their mood better (J7smyg1Czik [09:42], [10:13]); football players shaved time off the 40-yard dash and the 20-yard shuttle (the caption reads "1 point1 2 seconds", garbled, so the amount is not confirmed) (J7smyg1Czik [10:13], [10:44]); swimmers improved average turn time and added "five kicks" to their strokes (caption wording, unclear) (J7smyg1Czik [11:14]); tennis players improved serve accuracy (J7smyg1Czik [11:14]). From these she says adults need 7 to 8 hours but athletes need 9 to 10 (J7smyg1Czik [08:42], [09:12], [11:14]). She attributes the 9 to 10 hour figure to the extension studies (J7smyg1Czik [09:12]); the caption at [11:14] reads "athletes need 8 9 to 10 hours" (garbled). Inference: the figure is a synthesis across the studies, not a stated finding of any one of them. In the Q&A she acknowledges the extension studies measured time in bed, not sleep (J7smyg1Czik [25:57]).

**Why it works** — The speaker connects the gains to the effects listed earlier in her talk (reaction time, judgment, mood) but gives no direct mechanism for these results. Inference: the improvements may come from reduced chronic sleep loss in athletes who started short, not from sleeping more than needed; the talk does not report baseline sleep.

**When to apply** — As background when an athlete group is plainly short on sleep and the schedule allows more time in bed (for example, no early-morning facility constraints). Inference: this supports aiming to enable more time in bed before aiming at a specific hour target. Eric's baseline: sleep is not tracked and recovery is managed through training-load design alone (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit). The speaker also says sports limited by facility times, such as swimming and ice hockey, are hit hardest (J7smyg1Czik [23:55]).

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: the studies are reported second-hand with no citation, sample size or control, and measured time in bed, not sleep. Sample sizes, effect sizes (beyond the 9% shooting figures) and statistics are not given, and no control group is described in the talk. Time in bed was extended, so quality and total sleep were not measured. The athletes are Stanford athletes in four sports; there is no football-position, no NFL and no Baylor data. The 9 to 10 hours target should not be read as a requirement: in the Q&A she says people differ in how well they tolerate sleep loss, not in how much sleep they need (J7smyg1Czik [26:58]). A 2017 conference talk with no stated citation for the studies.

**Example** — The speaker's own: Stanford basketball players with a 9% increase in free throws and in three-point field goals after six weeks of 10 hours in bed (J7smyg1Czik [09:42]).

**Related** — [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]; [[heuristic--weekend-sleep-extension-signals-a-deficit]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]]; [[research-papers/vitale-2026-from-gpt-4-to-expert-endorsed-athlete-guidance-a-delphi-consensus-on-sleep-and-jet-lag]].

# Hours of Sleep Was the Strongest Predictor of Injury in a High School Athlete Study

**What it is** — The speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says high school athletes were followed for about 22 months and the number of hours of sleep gave the strongest prediction of the likelihood of injury (the caption reads "the number of odds of sleep", garbled); sleeping less than 8 hours raised injury likelihood by "1.7%" in the captions, a figure that may be garbled (for instance a ratio versus a percent) and should not be relied on (J7smyg1Czik [04:38], [05:08]). The speaker names no authors, journal or sample size. The speaker adds that reaction time and visual acuity worsen with too little sleep (caption: "reaction time is increase", garbled), which the speaker says makes injury more likely, and that the hormones needed for recovery are mostly secreted in sleep (J7smyg1Czik [05:08], [05:40]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's stated reasoning is slower reaction time and poorer visual acuity, plus reduced recovery hormones (J7smyg1Czik [05:08]). These are asserted as plausible links; the talk does not show them as mediators in the injury study. Inference: an association in adolescents can reflect other things that travel with short sleep (training volume, school load).

**When to apply** — As a reason to record sleep when injury data are collected, not as a prediction rule. Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model exists, and nothing objective is tracked for recovery or sleep (interview 2026-09-28, Q12 and Q23, Explicit). Inference: this claim, if confirmed against its source, is a candidate variable to log first; the source must be identified before it is cited.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: one unnamed study, high school athletes, the key number is unreadable in the captions, and the study design, injury definition and adjustment are not described. High school findings do not transfer to NCAA football without checking. Do not quote "1.7%". Related work in the library on college athletes' sleep and nap behavior should be consulted before using any sleep and injury statement.

**Example** — The speaker's own description: high school athletes followed for about 22 months, with hours of sleep as the strongest predictor of injury (J7smyg1Czik [04:38], [05:08]).

**Related** — [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]; [[heuristic--weekend-sleep-extension-signals-a-deficit]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]].

=== claim--sleep-restriction-lowered-testosterone-by-10-to-12-percent.md
confidence: untested
---

# Sleep Restriction Lowered Testosterone by 10 to 12% in Young College Students, the Speaker Says

**What it is** — The speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says growth hormone is secreted in deep sleep and testosterone is secreted while sleeping (with another peak while awake) (J7smyg1Czik [05:40]). The speaker describes an experiment in which young healthy college students had five fewer hours than eight in bed, and their testosterone levels fell by 10 to 12% (the caption reads "increased uh decreased by 10 to 12%", which looks like a spoken self-correction; the direction taken here is "decreased") (J7smyg1Czik [05:40], [06:12]). Normal aging loss is 1 to 2% per year, so the speaker says a 20-year-old after a week of restriction would look like a 31-year-old (J7smyg1Czik [06:12]). The speaker adds that sleep loss raises the hormones that break down muscle (J7smyg1Czik [06:42]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that the hormones are released in sleep, so less sleep means less of them. No study authors are named for any of these results. Inference: a reduction of 10 to 12% in an unnamed laboratory restriction study of young college students says little about an athlete's day-to-day testosterone.

**When to apply** — As background for why sleep is mentioned alongside recovery and hormones, never as a clinical test. Inference: the finding supports asking about sleep when an athlete reports poor recovery. Eric's baseline: nothing objective is tracked for recovery or sleep (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit); no hormone testing is in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: unnamed studies, sample sizes and durations not stated, and the caption garble in the key sentence. Young healthy college students (the speaker does not say how many or of which sex) in laboratory conditions. Existing library: a 2026 review of testosterone in athletes notes that sleep loss and sleep-disordered breathing may contribute to impaired testosterone regulation, and that evidence for sleep extension or melatonin as testosterone-enhancing interventions is not established, so do not present this as a treatment effect. The "age 31" comparison is the speaker's illustration, not a finding the speaker cites. Do not use this to interpret an athlete's own lab values.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a 20-year-old player after a week of lost sleep, with testosterone like that of a 31-year-old (J7smyg1Czik [06:12]).

**Related** — [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]; [[claim--sleep-hours-predicted-injury-in-high-school-athletes]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/lazarev-2026-testosterone-optimizing-strategies-in-athletes]] (partial tension on sleep as an intervention, not on the effect of loss).
=== framework--classify-chronotype-and-time-peak-performance.md
confidence: untested
---

# Classify Chronotype, Then Time Peak Performance Relative to When the Athlete Wakes

**What it is** — A method the speaker (a sleep scientist by the speaker's own words, "sleep scientists like me", J7smyg1Czik [01:03]; unnamed) describes from a study the speaker attributes to a "university of Birmingham" (caption spelling) group. Competition-level athletes completed a paper-and-pencil morning-evening questionnaire, which classified them as early, intermediate or late (night owl) (J7smyg1Czik [17:22], [17:52]). Performance tests were done six times across the day: the bleep test (endurance, oxygen uptake) and sprint times, along with athletes' own ratings (J7smyg1Czik [17:52], [18:24]). As a whole group, performance was lowest at 7 am and highest in the late afternoon; the captions read "between four and seven" without am or pm (J7smyg1Czik [18:24], [18:55]). By chronotype, early types peaked between noon and 2, intermediate types in the mid-afternoon, and late types between 7 and 8 in the evening (J7smyg1Czik [18:55]). Relative to waking, early and intermediate types peaked about 6 to 7 hours after waking, and late types 11 hours or more after (J7smyg1Czik [19:58], [20:30]). A further analysis of a large number of athletes in 12 teams predicted team peak by team makeup: a team of mostly late types (T3) peaked later than a team of mostly early types (T10) (J7smyg1Czik [20:30], [21:00]). In the Q&A the speaker says the body clock shifts mostly with light and can be moved with light boxes and melatonin, for example, in the speaker's words, "when we send the Lions to London" the clock was shifted to earlier bedtimes, and that this takes discipline (J7smyg1Czik [29:02]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that a biological clock decides whether someone is a night owl or morning lark, and everyone's peak therefore differs (J7smyg1Czik [16:51], [17:22]). The speaker's point is that a fixed wake time, imposed by a coach or schedule, does not shift when an individual peaks (J7smyg1Czik [19:58], [20:30]). The speaker gives no mechanism for the questionnaire's validity.

**When to apply** — When choosing the time of day for testing or high-stakes sessions, or when comparing an athlete's results across times. Inference: record each athlete's test time and, if the staff wishes, the questionnaire result, before comparing sessions; this matters for repeatable testing. Eric's baseline (course material, speaker unconfirmed, tagged Inferred): testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April"). Eric's baseline: Eric has no stated chronotype practice; the baseline is silent.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the study is relayed second-hand from a "university of Birmingham" group (J7smyg1Czik [17:22]) with no citation and no n stated, and the 12-team result is a prediction ("they predicted performance", [20:30]), not an observed outcome. Sample sizes are not stated for the questionnaire study; the only count is 12 teams. The study is competition-level athletes, not college football, and early-morning football practice and meal schedules are not under athletes' control. The speaker says the whole circadian advantage is "unexplored" (J7smyg1Czik [23:03]). The claim that a third of the teams the speaker talks to are not interested is the speaker's own experience (J7smyg1Czik [28:31]). A light and melatonin protocol was mentioned, not described; do not use it as a medical recommendation.

**Example** — The speaker's own: Team 3, mostly late types, versus Team 10, mostly early types; the speaker says if a morning game pitted them against each other, T3 would be at a biological disadvantage, and in the evening T10 would be (J7smyg1Czik [21:00], [21:32]).

**Related** — [[claim--circadian-misalignment-shifts-game-outcomes-nfl-and-baseball]]; [[heuristic--strategic-nap-lengths-and-when-not-to-nap]].
=== heuristic--strategic-nap-lengths-and-when-not-to-nap.md
confidence: untested
---

# Strategic Naps: 15 to 20 Minutes, 30 Minutes or 90 Minutes, and Not When Night Sleep Is Poor

**What it is** — In the Q&A, the speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says nine hours in bed means nine hours over a 24-hour period, so an athlete who cannot sleep it all at once can nap (J7smyg1Czik [29:33]). The speaker names three nap types: 15 to 20 minutes, after which you wake from light sleep and should feel refreshed; 30 minutes, which still ends in light sleep (stage two, the speaker says); and a 90-minute "granddaddy" nap that goes through light, deep and dream sleep, after which you wake spontaneously (J7smyg1Czik [29:33], [30:03]). The caution: if the athlete has trouble sleeping at night, a nap is "not a good thing," because "you're taking away from that sleep drive your homeostatic drive" (J7smyg1Czik [30:35]). The speaker also says trouble falling asleep in athletes usually comes from trying to sleep at an unusual time after crossing time zones (the example is four) or from heavy caffeine in the evening because games are in the evening (J7smyg1Czik [30:35]). The speaker adds that napping after training helps, since sleep consolidates learning and memory formed in training (J7smyg1Czik [25:25]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism for the length choice is the sleep stage you wake from: light sleep in the short naps, a full cycle in the 90-minute nap. The caution rests on the homeostatic sleep drive, which builds with time awake and which sleep consumes ("when you fall asleep you consume the Sleep drive", J7smyg1Czik [12:18]); a nap uses part of the drive that night sleep needs (J7smyg1Czik [12:18], [30:35]). What opposes the drive is the circadian alerting signal (J7smyg1Czik [12:48]). No study is cited for the nap lengths.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's schedule leaves time in bed short, and nighttime sleep is otherwise good. Inference: the three lengths give a short and a long option for a travel day or a long gap between sessions. Eric's baseline: no sleep or nap protocol is in the baseline; recovery is managed through training-load design alone (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the nap guidance is the speaker's practical advice with no data, population or study cited. Not for athletes with poor night sleep (the speaker's own rule). The talk does not address timing relative to training or competition. Inference: a long nap close to a session may leave an athlete groggy, but the speaker does not say so. Not a substitute for a clinical sleep evaluation. Naps are a make-up for total sleep, not a replacement for regular nights, since the speaker says deficits are cumulative (J7smyg1Czik [22:33]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: nine hours in bed counted over 24 hours, so a nap can make up time that one night did not (J7smyg1Czik [29:33]). Inference: a 15 to 20 minute nap fits a short gap between sessions; the 90-minute nap needs time to wake fully.

**Related** — [[heuristic--weekend-sleep-extension-signals-a-deficit]]; [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]] (NCAA Division I nap behavior).

confidence: untested
---

# If an Athlete Sleeps In on Days Off, Treat It as a Sign of a Weekday Deficit

**What it is** — In the Q&A, asked how to tell who needs eight hours and who nine, the speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says two things. First, people who say they can get by on five to seven hours are not people who need less; they tolerate deprivation better (J7smyg1Czik [26:58], [27:29]). Second, chronic deprivation makes you "lose your reference" for what being awake and alert feels like, so people think they are fine on five or six hours and never extend their sleep (J7smyg1Czik [27:29], [28:00]). Her check: find out whether the person sleeps in on days off or weekends, because that means they are not getting enough sleep on a regular basis and are "playing catch up" (J7smyg1Czik [28:00]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is that sleeping in is the body repaying a debt, and a person with a debt cannot rate their own alertness reliably. This is her assertion, with no study cited. Inference: because self-report is the problem, a behavioral sign (extra sleep on free days) is a more reliable cue than asking "do you feel rested."

**When to apply** — As a cheap screening question for athletes with fatigue complaints, poor test results or high injury concern: ask what time they wake on days off compared with training days. Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were abandoned because athletes learned to give consistent low-effort answers (Explicit, SportSmith piece, 2026-02-19), and nothing objective is tracked for sleep (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit). Inference: a one-time behavioral question is a different data type from a daily scale and avoids the same gaming problem, but that is untested.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: no data supporting the weekend-sleep cue are shown in the talk. Athletes may sleep in for reasons other than debt (an illness, a late game, travel). A talk speaker's rule of thumb should not replace a clinical evaluation of sleep problems, and the speaker herself separates sleep need from tolerance without giving a way to measure need. College athletes' days off are set by schedule and may not reflect free choice.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a person who says they need only five or six hours but sleeps in at the weekend, which she reads as a regular deficit (J7smyg1Czik [27:29], [28:00]).

**Related** — [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]; [[claim--sleep-extension-improved-stanford-athlete-performance]]; [[claim--wellness-questionnaires-collapse-to-one-number]] (why self-report scales fail). Existing library: [[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]].

16	
17	**What it is** — The speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) summarizes the Stanford sleep-extension studies: athletes were given 10 hours in bed for six weeks, wore actigraphs, kept sleep diaries, and were tested near the end of the six weeks (J7smyg1Czik [09:12], [09:42]). Reported results: basketball players had a significant reduction in sprint times and a 9% increase in both free throws and three-point field goals, were less sleepy, and rated their mood better (J7smyg1Czik [09:42], [10:13]); football players shaved time off the 40-yard dash and the 20-yard shuttle (the caption reads "1 point1 2 seconds", garbled, so the amount is not confirmed) (J7smyg1Czik [10:13], [10:44]); swimmers improved average turn time and added "five kicks" to their strokes (caption wording, unclear) (J7smyg1Czik [11:14]); tennis players improved serve accuracy (J7smyg1Czik [11:14]). From these she says adults need 7 to 8 hours but athletes need 9 to 10 (J7smyg1Czik [08:42], [09:12], [11:14]). She attributes the 9 to 10 hour figure to the extension studies (J7smyg1Czik [09:12]); the caption at [11:14] reads "athletes need 8 9 to 10 hours" (garbled). Inference: the figure is a synthesis across the studies, not a stated finding of any one of them. In the Q&A she acknowledges the extension studies measured time in bed, not sleep (J7smyg1Czik [25:57]).
18	
19	**Why it works** — The speaker connects the gains to the effects listed earlier in her talk (reaction time, judgment, mood) but gives no direct mechanism for these results. Inference: the improvements may come from reduced chronic sleep loss in athletes who started short, not from sleeping more than needed; the talk does not report baseline sleep.
20	
21	**When to apply** — As background when an athlete group is plainly short on sleep and the schedule allows more time in bed (for example, no early-morning facility constraints). Inference: this supports aiming to enable more time in bed before aiming at a specific hour target. Eric's baseline: sleep is not tracked and recovery is managed through training-load design alone (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit). The speaker also says sports limited by facility times, such as swimming and ice hockey, are hit hardest (J7smyg1Czik [23:55]).
22	
23	**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: the studies are reported second-hand with no citation, sample size or control, and measured time in bed, not sleep. Sample sizes, effect sizes (beyond the 9% shooting figures) and statistics are not given, and no control group is described in the talk. Time in bed was extended, so quality and total sleep were not measured. The athletes are Stanford athletes in four sports; there is no football-position, no NFL and no Baylor data. The 9 to 10 hours target should not be read as a requirement: in the Q&A she says people differ in how well they tolerate sleep loss, not in how much sleep they need (J7smyg1Czik [26:58]). A 2017 conference talk with no stated citation for the studies.

16	
17	**What it is** — In the Q&A, asked how to tell who needs eight hours and who nine, the speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says two things. First, people who say they can get by on five to seven hours are not people who need less; they tolerate deprivation better (J7smyg1Czik [26:58], [27:29]). Second, chronic deprivation makes you "lose your reference" for what being awake and alert feels like, so people think they are fine on five or six hours and never extend their sleep (J7smyg1Czik [27:29], [28:00]). Her check: find out whether the person sleeps in on days off or weekends, because that means they are not getting enough sleep on a regular basis and are "playing catch up" (J7smyg1Czik [28:00]).
18	
19	**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is that sleeping in is the body repaying a debt, and a person with a debt cannot rate their own alertness reliably. This is her assertion, with no study cited. Inference: because self-report is the problem, a behavioral sign (extra sleep on free days) is a more reliable cue than asking "do you feel rested."
20	
21	**When to apply** — As a cheap screening question for athletes with fatigue complaints, poor test results or high injury concern: ask what time they wake on days off compared with training days. Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were abandoned because athletes learned to give consistent low-effort answers (Explicit, SportSmith piece, 2026-02-19), and nothing objective is tracked for sleep (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit). Inference: a one-time behavioral question is a different data type from a daily scale and avoids the same gaming problem, but that is untested.
22	
23	**When NOT to apply** — Untested: no data supporting the weekend-sleep cue are shown in the talk. Athletes may sleep in for reasons other than debt (an illness, a late game, travel). A talk speaker's rule of thumb should not replace a clinical evaluation of sleep problems, and the speaker herself separates sleep need from tolerance without giving a way to measure need. College athletes' days off are set by schedule and may not reflect free choice.
24	
25	**Example** — The speaker's own: a person who says they need only five or six hours but sleeps in at the weekend, which she reads as a regular deficit (J7smyg1Czik [27:29], [28:00]).

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

# Sleep Deficits Accumulate, and Three Nights of Recovery Sleep Do Not Fully Erase Them

**What it is** — The speaker, a sleep scientist (unnamed in the captions) who elsewhere in the talk says "our lab at Henry Ford" (J7smyg1Czik [07:42]), says that getting six to seven hours instead of eight "doubles or triples" normal reaction time, which the talk puts at about a quarter of a second (J7smyg1Czik [01:33]). The talk shows a sleep deprivation study in which the same individuals go through different conditions: seven days of 7 hours in bed per the captions (the summary phrase "7 five versus 3 hours" is garbled) versus nine hours in bed, each followed by three days of nine-hour recovery sleep (J7smyg1Czik [02:05], [02:36]). Mean speed and the number of lapses worsened as days of deficit increased; after three recovery days at nine hours in bed, the restricted group recovered but "never as good as" people who get nine hours regularly (J7smyg1Czik [02:36]). The speaker concludes that deficits are cumulative and "non-recoverable" over a short window, so sleep before a game is not enough (J7smyg1Czik [22:33]), and says athletes tend to sleep poorly right before games because of anxiety or a strange environment (J7smyg1Czik [03:07]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for accumulation; the study result is shown without one. Inference: the result as stated means a short recovery block does not return performance to the level of consistently well-rested people, so the amount of regular sleep leading up to an event matters more than the last night.

**When to apply** — When advising athletes before a competition or travel block: focus on sleep across the preceding days, not only the night before. Inference: this supports looking at multi-night sleep, if it were measured. Eric's baseline: recovery is managed through training-load design alone and nothing objective is tracked, sleep included (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit). The talk's finding would need some sleep measure to act on; none exists in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — The study is not cited, and its sample size, population and test are not stated; the design numbers are garbled in the captions (7 hours in bed as captioned, "7 five versus 3 hours"). Confidence is untested. "Non-recoverable" is the speaker's wording for a three-day test; the talk does not follow recovery beyond three days. Auto-caption talk from 2017; the results were presented by a speaker with a sleep-lab affiliation, not as a peer-reviewed table. It does not apply as a measurement tool: it shows an effect in healthy adults under restriction, not a sleep target for Baylor athletes.

**Example** — The speaker's own: restricted-time-in-bed participants after three nine-hour recovery nights compared with participants who had nine hours throughout (J7smyg1Czik [02:36]).

**Related** — [[claim--sleep-extension-improved-stanford-athlete-performance]]; [[heuristic--weekend-sleep-extension-signals-a-deficit]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]] (NCAA Division I sleep and nap behavior).

# A Quarterback-Specific Model by Transfer Learning: Reported Failure

**What it is** — Burke's fourth variant tries to capture one passer's tendencies. The motive he gives: "we don't have enough data for individual quarterbacks, they just don't have enough pass attempts" (EeBgUCYhezc [18:20]). The method (EeBgUCYhezc [18:50]):

1. Train all layers on the full data set, all quarterbacks.
2. Freeze the base layers.
3. Retrain on one quarterback only.

He compares the shared layers to a common intuitive sense of physics (everyone can drive without crashing) and the retrained layers to individual executive decision-making (EeBgUCYhezc [19:21]). The result: "not as well as I'd hoped". Drew Brees (as named) was the most similar quarterback to Drew Brees, but some of the best-performing quarterbacks were the least similar and some of the poorest performers the most similar, on target-decision similarity (EeBgUCYhezc [19:51]). He offers an explanation that Brees threw to running backs by design, while others do so "as a last resort" (EeBgUCYhezc [20:22]; the caption text here is garbled, so the explanation is uncertain). He reports it despite the result, calling this variant "pretty experimental" (EeBgUCYhezc [18:20]).

**Why it works** — It did not work as hoped, so there is no mechanism to give for success. The speaker gives the brain analogy above only as intent. Inference: the speaker says individual passers lack enough attempts, so retraining on one passer likely leaves too little to fit person-specific layers.

**When to apply** — As a cautionary case when someone proposes a per-athlete model from a small pooled data set (a single Baylor quarterback, one athlete's force-plate history). Ask first what the athlete-level sample size is and how similarity will be checked.

Eric's baseline: individual thresholds use "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q2a.) Inference: that is a simple within-person method, not a pooled-model fine-tune.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one reported attempt, in one data set (2016 to 2018 NFL passes), with no reported metric beyond the similarity ranking, so it should not be cited as proof that transfer learning cannot work for individualized models. It is also not a recommendation to use it. The speaker's explanation for the odd similarity ordering is unverified.

**Example** — The talk's own: the top five and bottom five "similar quarterbacks" ranking, in which Brees is most similar to himself (EeBgUCYhezc [19:51]).

**Related** — [[framework--deepqb-receiver-target-model-inputs-and-four-variants]] (variant 4 is this); [[claim--deepqb-target-accuracy-60-percent-against-20-percent-chance]].

# DeepQB Picks the Targeted Receiver About 60 Percent of the Time, Triple Chance

**What it is** — Burke reports that variant 1 predicts which receiver the quarterback throws to "just about 60%" of the time on the test set; the no-information guess would be one in five, 20 percent, so "we're tripling that information gain" (EeBgUCYhezc [07:48]). Completion percentage is 74 percent when the quarterback throws to the model's recommended receiver and 55 percent when he throws to any other, "a factor of 1.4" (EeBgUCYhezc [08:50]).

The speaker explains why 60 percent is not a poor score: a quarterback "is never going to do this thing twice in a row" given the same situation, so there is natural variance no model removes, and the defense's purpose is to make sure no single receiver is far more favorable than the others, which drives the number down (EeBgUCYhezc [08:19]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for why completion differs by 74 versus 55. Inference: the model's top choice is the receiver with the best separation and angles, so agreement partly reflects an easier throw, not that the quarterback's choice is the cause of the difference; the talk does not separate the two.

**When to apply** — When judging any "who gets the ball" or "what happens next" model, state the chance baseline (here 1 in 5) before the accuracy, as the speaker does. Use the 74 versus 55 split to ask whether the model's recommendation carries outcome information.

Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q3.) Inference: the question here is a decision-review one (was this the right target), and a score only earns its place if staff would act on a flagged play.

**When NOT to apply** — The 60 percent is the speaker's own framing of an acceptable result, from one test period (2018 through week 12) and NFL data (EeBgUCYhezc [05:13], [07:48]). There is no confidence interval, and no comparison with a simple baseline other than chance (such as "throw to the open receiver"). Agreement with the model later correlated slightly negatively with production (see [[heuristic--credit-yards-above-expected-to-the-passer-with-selection-bias-caveat]]), so high agreement is not a quality score by itself. The talk gives no college or Baylor-level numbers.

**Example** — The speaker's own examples: an easy play where the model gives a crossing receiver an 80 percent target chance (EeBgUCYhezc [09:50]); a checkdown given 8 percent while a deeper open receiver gets 77 percent, which the speaker reads as a probable poor decision (EeBgUCYhezc [10:52]); and a covered receiver the quarterback throws to anyway, where the model agrees because of a velocity advantage and inside leverage, showing that proximity alone does not decide the target (EeBgUCYhezc [11:23], [11:53]).

**Related** — [[framework--deepqb-receiver-target-model-inputs-and-four-variants]]; [[framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split]].

# Checking an Outcome-Probability Model: Split by What Happened, Then Calibrate

**What it is** — Burke's variant 3 predicts complete, incomplete or intercepted for the targeted pass. He checks it two ways (EeBgUCYhezc [14:38], [15:40], [16:12]):

1. Split plays by what actually happened and read the average predicted completion probability: 79 percent for actual completions, 56 percent for actual incompletions (targeted passes only, so the numbers look high).
2. A calibration chart for completion probability, which he calls "fairly well calibrated".

He then reads interceptions with care. The rate is "a low base rate, very very random event" (tipped passes, bobbles, wind), so decision-making is only one factor, and passers vary within "a very tight window" of estimated interception probability (EeBgUCYhezc [17:13], [17:43]). Jameis Winston (name as in captions) had the highest estimated and actual 2018 rate through week 12, but Burke judged most of it came "from inaccurate throws compared to poor decision making" (EeBgUCYhezc [17:43]). Two case plays (Winston, and Derek Carr on second and two against what he reads as triple or quadruple coverage) are shown as poor decisions (EeBgUCYhezc [16:43], [17:13]).

In Q&A he concedes a class imbalance problem (interceptions are rare) and did not rebalance, because the model does "so many different things all at once" and time was short; he says he did take measures for his earlier Hall of Fame model, "to make sure that the those low rate cases are over represented in the data but not here" (EeBgUCYhezc [24:36], [25:08]).

**Why it works** — The outcome split is a face-validity check: Inference: a model with signal should give higher completion probability where completions happened. The speaker gives no further mechanism. Inference: calibration matters when the output will be read as a probability by a coach, because a ranked score can look good while its probabilities are off.

**When to apply** — Any model whose output a staff member will read as "chance of X". Run both checks before showing it, and say when an outcome is too rare to read (Inference: a handful of interceptions per passer in a season is below what supports a person-level claim).

Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Eric-authored, Nordbord piece, in method-baseline.md). Inference: the same logic applies to model outputs; a probability that is not checked is not yet usable.

**When NOT to apply** — The 79 versus 56 numbers are the speaker's report on one test period; no calibration error value is given (EeBgUCYhezc [16:12]). The interception probabilities are low and the class imbalance was not corrected, so interception results should not drive a decision on a passer (EeBgUCYhezc [24:36]). The decision-versus-accuracy split for Winston is an assertion without a measured breakdown in the talk.

**Example** — The speaker's: the 2018 Winston interception rate, assigned mostly to inaccurate throws, not poor decisions (EeBgUCYhezc [17:43]).

# DeepQB: Receiver-Level Inputs and Four Model Variants

**What it is** — Brian Burke (name as stated in the host introduction, EeBgUCYhezc [00:00]) presents DeepQB, a feed-forward neural network, which the speaker calls "a relatively vanilla type of deep learning application", applied to NFL Next Gen Stats (NGS) player tracking data (EeBgUCYhezc [03:42], [04:12]). One architecture answers four questions (EeBgUCYhezc [04:12], [04:43]):

1. Variant 1: which of the five eligible receivers the quarterback targets (target probability).
2. Variant 2: expected yards on the play.
3. Variant 3: outcome probability (complete, incomplete, intercepted).
4. Variant 4: variant 1 tailored to one quarterback (see [[case-study--deepqb-quarterback-specific-transfer-learning-did-not-work]]).

**Inputs.** The feature vector is arranged by the five eligible receivers: absolute position, position relative to the quarterback, velocity, orientation, and receiver type (wide receiver, tight end, running back) (EeBgUCYhezc [06:15]). It adds the nearest two defenders in coverage (absolute and relative position, velocities, accelerations, orientations), then play context: game state, down, distance, yard line, play action, a 1/0 flag for quarterback duress, and quarterback velocity at release (EeBgUCYhezc [06:15], [06:46]). The speaker stresses that the NGS data are "extremely clean" and available about 10 seconds after the play (EeBgUCYhezc [05:44]).

**Data and split.** More than 45,000 targeted passes only (the model only sees whom the quarterback chose to throw to), drawn from 2016 through 2018 through week 12 of 2018, split into training, validation and test sets; all reported results are from the test set, 2018 through week 12 (EeBgUCYhezc [04:43], [05:13]).

**Mirror-image augmentation.** Each play is also included flipped left-right in the training set, to teach symmetry. The speaker names the flaw: quarterback handedness (EeBgUCYhezc [06:46], [07:16]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives one reason for the single architecture: the speaker found "the architecture of the model was optimum for a wide variety of applications" because it suited the structure of the data, so the same network could be asked different questions (EeBgUCYhezc [04:12]). The speaker gives no mechanism for why mirroring helps beyond the symmetry intent. Inference: arranging inputs per receiver lets the same weights score each of the five targets, which is why one model can serve several outputs.

**When to apply** — As a reference design when someone proposes a model of a passer's decision from play-level positional data: check that the inputs describe each option (receiver and nearest defenders), the context (down, distance, duress), and that results are scored only on a held-out period.

Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." (Eric-authored SportSmith, in method-baseline.md.) Inference: this model needs league-grade per-play tracking at scale (45,000+ passes), which is a large collection cost; Eric's baseline contains no football position-tracking method, so there is nothing of his own to compare it with.

**When NOT to apply** — NFL tracking data of a quality Baylor does not hold; the speaker built this on 2016 to 2018 NFL passes. It sees positions, speed and orientation only: "no vertical information" and no "hands" (EeBgUCYhezc [22:01]).
